prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I tried one or two but they were stale and broke like sticks or crumbled when I rolled them and lighting a match was useless nor could I put them back in the refrigerator— it was too late for that—even licking them filled my mouth with ground-up outer leaf, product of Lancaster or eastern Virginia, so schooled I am with cigars, it comes in the blood, and I threw handfuls of them into the street from three floors up and, to my horror, sitting on my stoop were four or five street people who ran to catch them as if they were suddenly rich, and I apologize for that, no one should be degraded that way, my hands were crazy, and I ran down to explain but they were smoking already nor did I have anything to give them since we were living on beans ourselves, I sat and smoked too, and once in a while we looked up at the open window, and one of us spit into his empty can. We were visionaries.

outputs.L1: I tried one or two, but they were stale: they snapped like sticks or crumbled when I rolled them, and striking a match was useless. Nor could I put them back in the refrigerator—it was too late for that. Even licking them filled my mouth with ground-up outer leaf, the product of Lancaster or eastern Virginia; so well schooled am I in cigars—it comes in the blood. I threw handfuls of them into the street from three floors up and, to my horror, four or five street people sitting on my stoop ran to catch them as if they had suddenly become rich. I apologize for that. No one should be degraded in such a way. My hands were crazy, and I ran downstairs to explain, but they were already smoking. Nor did I have anything to give them, since we ourselves were living on beans. I sat and smoked, too, and every so often we looked up at the open window, and one of us spat into his empty can. We were visionaries.
outputs.L2: I sampled a couple, but they were so dry that they snapped like twigs or fell apart whenever I tried to roll them. A match did no good, and returning them to the refrigerator was pointless by then. Even moistening them with my tongue left my mouth full of shredded wrapper leaf—grown in Lancaster or perhaps eastern Virginia. I know cigars instinctively; that knowledge is inherited. From a third-floor window, I flung them by the handful into the road, only to discover, with horror, four or five homeless people seated on my front steps. They scrambled after the cigars as though they had stumbled upon a fortune. I am sorry for doing that; no human being ought to be humiliated in such a fashion. My hands had acted wildly. I hurried downstairs to explain, but they had already begun smoking. I had nothing else to offer, because we ourselves were surviving on beans. So I joined them and smoked, and now and then we all glanced toward the open window above. One of us spat into his empty tin. We were seers.

outputs.L4:
I can’t reconstruct the original source passage from its summary, but I can provide a new, original version of the scene:

When I opened the cigar box, the smell told me at once that something was wrong. The cigars had dried into brittle brown sticks, their wrappers cracked and their flavor spoiled beyond recovery. I tried one nevertheless, but the smoke was harsh and bitter. Annoyed by the waste, I carried the box to an upstairs window and flung the cigars into the street.

Almost immediately, several poorly dressed men and women hurried toward them. They stooped over the pavement, gathering the discarded cigars as though they were coins. Watching them scramble for what I had rejected filled me with shame. My moment of irritation had become a spectacle of their need.

I went downstairs and stepped outside.

“Friends,” I said, approaching them, “I owe you an apology. Those cigars are stale. I threw them away because they are scarcely fit to smoke.”

One of the men examined the cigar in his hand and smiled. “They may not be fit for you,” he said, “but they will do well enough for us.”

There was no accusation in his voice, which made his answer harder to bear. I explained again that I had not meant to insult anyone. Then, uncertain what else to do, I took one of the cigars from the ground, struck a match, and lit it. The others laughed, and soon matches were passing from hand to hand.

We stood together in the street, drawing on those miserable cigars and pretending they were finer than they were. The smoke stung our eyes and caught in our throats, yet no one complained. For a few minutes poverty, embarrassment, and rank lost their authority over us. We were simply a circle of people sharing tobacco, jokes, and the warmth of one another’s company.

The world had given us little to celebrate, but we celebrated anyway. Through the bitter smoke we became visionaries, seeing not the rags, the hunger, or the indignity of the moment, but a fellowship that made us equal.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about finding a box of stale cigars, throwing them from an apartment window, and unexpectedly sharing a smoke with homeless people below.
counterfactuals.output:
In the back of a closet, behind winter coats and a suitcase with one broken wheel, I found the box of cigars my father had forgotten to finish. They lay in their paper sleeves like small, dried branches, their tobacco gone pale with years, their sweetness turned to dust. I opened the window and threw them out one by one, not from anger exactly, but from the need to watch something leave me. They spun through the evening, little brown propellers, landing on the sidewalk where three people had arranged their blankets beneath the awning.

One man picked up a cigar and held it to his ear as if listening for weather. A woman laughed. Another struck a match against the brick, and soon all three were smoking, solemn as kings in a ruined court. I went downstairs to apologize, though I carried nothing but the old silver cutter from the box.

They made room for me.

The cigars were terrible—bitter, dry, reluctant to burn—but we passed them beneath the trembling streetlight. Smoke lifted between us, blue and temporary, taking the shapes of roofs, ships, angels with nowhere to sleep. No one asked whose they had been. No one asked where any of us were going. For a few minutes, the city kept its distance, and we sat together in the strange inheritance of what had fallen: three strangers, myself, and the stale fire of the dead, glowing warmly in our hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single long, breathless paragraph narrated by a poor but reflective cigar lover whose impulsive act leads to a moment of fellowship and shame.
counterfactuals.output: I had only three copper coins in my pocket, none of them friendly enough to become supper, and yet when I passed the tobacconist’s window and saw the dark cigars lying in their cedar boxes like little sealed promises of warmth and dignity, I felt that old hunger which is not of the belly but of the soul pretending it has a drawing room, a velvet chair, an hour free from rent and rain, and before good sense could seize my wrist I slipped inside, laid down all three coins, and asked for the cheapest crooked cigar in the case, then hurried beneath the railway arch to light it, though the wind fought me and my matches were damp, until a ragged old porter sheltering there cupped his hands around mine and brought the flame alive, smiling as if we had performed a sacred office together, and because joy makes a rich man of any fool I broke the cigar in two and gave him half, and we stood shoulder to shoulder drawing bitter smoke, coughing, laughing, speaking of Havana though neither of us had traveled farther than the workhouse gates, and for a few blessed minutes the dripping stones became a club, the passing carriages our servants, the smoke itself a blue banner of brotherhood, but then my little daughter came running through the rain with her shoes split at the toes, crying that Mother had sent her to find me because there was no coal and the baby was cold, and I saw her eyes move from my empty hands to the cigar between my fingers, saw too the porter quietly lower his half as though it had turned to ash in his mouth, and all our imagined splendor collapsed at once, leaving only two poor men beneath an arch, one kind and one selfish, though I could no longer tell which was which, and I crushed the ember under my heel with such force that it seemed I might grind my whole foolish heart into the mud, while the porter, without reproach, pressed his last lump of coal money into my daughter’s palm, thereby sharing with me not merely his poverty but the unbearable knowledge that fellowship can make a man feel noble for an instant and ashamed for the rest of his life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Tell a surreal, bittersweet story in first person involving crumbling cigars, an open third-floor window, street people, beans, and an empty can; end with “We were visionaries.”
counterfactuals.output:
Every Thursday, my father mailed me a cigar.

He had been dead for eleven years, but the packages kept arriving: small brown boxes tied with blue thread, no return address, each containing a cigar already crumbling into fragrant black leaves. I never smoked them. I kept them in a sugar bowl beside the open third-floor window, where the wind carried pieces away one by one.

Below, the street people gathered at dusk. They had names for the pigeons and prophecies for the buses. Mara, who wore six wedding veils, claimed the moon was an unpaid electric bill. Old Penn folded traffic sounds into invisible envelopes. A boy called Beans slept under the awning and insisted he had been born from a tin of beans during a thunderstorm.

One winter evening, I cooked everything left in my cupboard: three handfuls of beans, half an onion, and the last cigar’s worth of tobacco, which fell into the pot when the wind tipped the sugar bowl. The stew smelled like my father’s coat.

I lowered it from the open window in a bucket.

They ate without complaint. Even the empty can beside Beans seemed to eat, filling itself with rain, then stars, then the faint music of a ballroom none of us could see. For a moment my father stood among them, young and embarrassed, holding out his hands as if he had finally remembered what he meant to give me.

Then the bucket rope snapped.

The pot fell upward.

We watched it vanish into the snow, spilling beans across the sky. By morning, every rooftop had sprouted green vines, though it was January, though the city had forgotten how to believe in spring.

Mara laughed. Beans cried. I closed the window because the room had become unbearably cold.

Years later, they demolished the building. I found the empty can in the rubble, still warm, humming my father’s voice. I held it to my ear, and heard all of us below that window—hungry, foolish, briefly fed.

We were visionaries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness literary monologue about poverty, dignity, and human connection, using stale tobacco as the central image.
counterfactuals.output:
The tobacco has gone stale again, though stale is only a word for something that has waited longer than hope expected it to. I pinch it from the tin—old biscuit tin, blue once, with a painted ship crossing a sea no ship could cross—and it comes apart between my fingers like attic dust, like the dry brown soil behind the factory where nothing grew but nettles and rumors. Still, I roll it. Carefully. Dignity is often just this: making a straight cigarette from crumbs.

The paper tears. Of course it tears. Everything thin and meant to hold us tears eventually—paper, pockets, patience, the skin over the knuckles. I lick the edge and try again. My tongue tastes bitterness before the match is struck.

Across the room, Mara is sleeping with her coat over her feet. I told her the stove was enough. She told me she liked the weight of the coat. We are courteous with our lies. That may be another name for love.

People imagine poverty as emptiness, but it is crowded, crowded: every coin shouting its destination, every cupboard haunted by meals not made, every knock at the door swelling into a verdict. Even silence costs something. Even sleep comes with calculations. If I wake at six, I can walk instead of taking the bus; if I walk, the soles may last until Friday; if they split, cardboard; if it rains, then what? Then what, then what—the little refrain of the poor, our hymn without a melody.

The match flares beautifully. That is the insult of it. Such a small gold palace in my hand. For one second I own fire.

I draw in, and the tobacco tastes of drawers shut too long, of dead leaves, of the pockets of men who stood outside hiring gates pretending not to be cold. My father smoked tobacco like this. He would tap the tin twice before opening it, as though asking permission. He had hands built for lifting and a voice built for apology. When he gave me my first cigarette, he said, Don’t make a habit of taking what’s offered. I thought he meant smoking.

Perhaps he meant the whole world.

The smoke moves toward the ceiling, finds every crack, touches what I cannot reach. Mara stirs. “You’ll burn the place down,” she murmurs.

“What place?”

She opens one eye, and there it is: the answer. This place. This room with its damp constellation, its chair with three honest legs and one liar, its single cup we rinse between us. This place because we are in it. This place because she is sleeping and I am keeping watch, though against what I do not know. Hunger has no footsteps. Shame carries a key.

I hand her the cigarette. She sits up, takes it without thanks because thanks would make it charity, and we have rules. She draws deeply, coughs, laughs. The laugh is rough and sudden and more nourishing than anything in the cupboard.

“Awful,” she says.

“The finest.”

“Imported?”

“From the Empire of Dust.”

She passes it back, and our fingers touch—just the blunt contact of skin, nothing a rich person would notice. But there are nights when touch is the only proof that the body has not been repossessed. Her hand is warm. Mine is not. Between them, the cigarette burns with a small, stubborn redness.

We smoke it down to nearly nothing. Waste is a luxury too. At the end I hold the butt with a pin, then she scolds me, then takes it and does the same. Outside, someone drags a bottle cart over the stones. Somewhere a baby cries with the confidence of a creature that believes an answer must come.

And perhaps one does. Not rescue, no. Rescue is a clean word, a word in polished shoes. But an answer: half a blanket, half a cigarette, half a joke offered across the dark. A shoulder. A name spoken gently. The last bitterness passed from mouth to mouth until, by being shared, it becomes almost warmth.

The tobacco is stale. Our breath is visible. Morning is still hours away.

“Leave some for tomorrow,” Mara says.

There is almost nothing left.

I tap the ash into the saucer and say, “Of course.”

Another courteous lie, but she smiles, and for a moment we are not begging anything from the world. For a moment we are giving it smoke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unpunctuated-feeling prose poem in which the speaker tosses unusable cigars into the street, regrets degrading the people who catch them, then goes downstairs and joins them.
counterfactuals.output:
from the high window I throw the split cigars  
the damp ones the bitter ones the ones no flame will keep  
and below hands rise from the street  
quick as birds around a crust  

I laugh and call them beggars  
as if hunger were a name I had invented  
as if my height were virtue  
as if the glass between us made me clean  

then shame enters softly  
smelling of cold tobacco and rain  

I leave the room  
take the stairs two at a time  
and out beneath my own window  
kneel among them  

we gather what has fallen  
we strike our matches against the same stone  
we cup the little failures of fire  
in our common hands
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
